requirements.requirement: Mount /tmp with noexec, nosuid, and nodev behavior, persisting across reboot.
requirements.summary: Before the change, /tmp was part of the root filesystem. After configuration and a verified reboot, it was a tmpfs mounted with nosuid,nodev,noexec. Post-reboot behavioral probes directly showed execution and device access denied, setuid ineffective, normal data access working, and the persistent fstab entry present.

requirements.requirement: Mount /dev/shm with noexec, nosuid, and nodev behavior, persisting across reboot.
requirements.summary: After a verified reboot, /dev/shm remained a tmpfs mounted with nosuid,nodev,noexec. Post-reboot probes directly demonstrated execution and device access denial, ignored setuid behavior, successful normal data access, and a valid persistent fstab entry.

requirements.requirement: Keep the installed operating-system release and kernel and use a compatible implementation.
requirements.summary: AlmaLinux 9.6 and kernel 5.14.0-570.12.1.el9_6.x86_64 were identical before and after execution. The implementation used native fstab, tmpfs, mount, and systemd facilities; package health remained clean and no package installation or platform replacement occurred.

overall_summary: All material outcomes are satisfied. Both mounts have the required security behavior and survived an observed reboot; the operating-system release and kernel were preserved. The provider restart protocol is complete for node1: healthy pre-restart state, acknowledged restart, changed boot identity, and recovered system, mount, data, and service state. Fixed lifecycle boot identities independently corroborate the reboot.

operational_hygiene.summary: No unnecessary mutations were identified. The fstab edit and rollback backup directly supported the persistent configuration; daemon reloads and mount changes applied it. Behavioral tests used bounded temporary files and briefly enabled exec solely to test nosuid, then restored hardening and removed probes. The scheduled reboot was required both to verify persistence and to satisfy the restart protocol. Lifecycle evidence shows no failed services, new network exposure, or package damage; temporary-file changes are expected consequences of the required reboot and new /tmp tmpfs.
